verses: At dusk the Ting star passed on to the west, And field work for the year was laid to rest. At Ch'u the duke his palace took in hand, And by the sun fixed how its walls should stand. All round about he planted many a tree,-- Hazels and chestnuts, t'ung and tzu, and i, And varnish trees. The grove would yield erelong Abundant wood for lutes, to aid the voice of song.

He climbed those ruined walls, thence to inspect The site he wished for Ch'u-ch'iu to select. His glance the land from Ch'u to T'ang mapped out Noting the hills and smaller heights about, He then came down, the mulberry trees to view, And judged the soil, and learned its nature true. These things once done, he asked the tortoise shell, Answer auspicious got,--and all succeeded well.

Thereafter, when there fell the copious showers, He often called his groom, and in the hours Of early dawn afield by starlight drove Among the laborers, and to cheer them strove. And many ways he had, not this alone, In which his character distinguished shone, To duty bound, assiduous in his cares;-- And blessing came,--three thousand steeds and mares.
